metadata.title: Does test-based school accountability have an impact on student achievement and equity in education?

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study pools PISA microdata across four cycles (2006, 2009, 2012, 2015) into a country-level panel and estimates regression models using the Stata Repest command. Repest is used to account for PISA’s complex survey design and sampling variation, and it also incorporates the plausible values (5 or 10 PVs per test score) by averaging across plausible values and adding imputation error to the variance. The paper reports that observation weights are re-estimated so each country contributes with the same weight to the final least-squares estimates, and it uses clustered standard errors at the country level. For country-level inference, it further bootstraps standard errors by repeatedly re-estimating models while leaving one country out at a time (jackknife-style country resampling).

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper explicitly states that Repest accounts for PISA plausible values (averaging across PVs and adding imputation error), but it does not describe a separate missing-data strategy for questionnaire or covariate missingness. Because the dependent variables are PV-based PISA scores and the methodology focuses on PV variance handling rather than covariate missingness, the missing-data handling for predictors is not documented in the provided text. This is a reporting gap for analysts who need to know whether missing covariates were imputed or cases were excluded.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The authors use PISA 2006–2015 microdata (four PISA cycles) and construct a pooled country-level panel by merging student achievement PVs (mathematics; and also reading/science in annex analyses) with student, school, and institutional questionnaire information. They restrict the analytic sample to countries that have at least two PISA implementations during 2006–2015 and have available information about school practices (including test-based accountability measures from the school/head teacher questionnaire). They also exclude earlier PISA cycles because the questionnaire wording for accountability items is not comparable prior to 2006. For estimation, they use the available pooled sample for the specified countries and apply Repest to account for PVs and complex survey design; standard errors are clustered at the country level and country-level inference uses leave-one-country-out bootstrapping.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper uses PISA 2006–2015 to study whether test-based school accountability affects student achievement and equity, and whether school autonomy moderates these relationships. The authors build a pooled country-level panel by merging student PV-based achievement scores (mathematics as the main dependent variable; reading and science in annexes) with student SES (ESCS) and school/head teacher questionnaire measures of accountability and autonomy. They estimate regression models using the Stata Repest command to account for PISA’s complex survey design and plausible values, and they cluster standard errors at the country level; for country-level uncertainty they bootstrap by leaving one country out at a time. Across all countries, they find no conclusive evidence that accountability is associated with achievement or inequality in mathematics (and broadly similar patterns for reading), while science shows a positive average association alongside increased inequality driven by lower- and middle-income countries. For low- and middle-income countries, accountability is associated with higher performance in mathematics and science, but with a trade-off of increased inequality, and autonomy in curriculum/assessment appears to strengthen the positive accountability–achievement association.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD working paper that applies PISA data with regression-based panel methods rather than training machine-learning predictive models. As a result, the extraction contains no ML algorithms and no ML-style predictive performance metrics to tabulate as StructuredFinding rows. The main results are therefore summarized narratively in outcome_summary, while main_findings remains empty.
